title: Google IT Support Certificate Guide
description: The Google IT Support Professional Certificate is the original Google Career Certificate — a six-course, zero-prerequisite program on Coursera covering troubleshooting and customer support, networking, operating systems, system administration and security basics, with browser-based VM labs and, since the 2025 refresh, using AI in support work. It is ACE-approved for up to 15 college credits, and completing it plus passing both CompTIA A+ exams earns a dual Google and CompTIA badge.
audience: Absolute beginners deciding whether IT is for them, and career changers from retail, service, or any non-technical field who need a structured curriculum more than they need another YouTube playlist. No degree, no experience, just consistent weekly hours.
why_get_it: It is the cheapest legitimate answer to "is IT actually for me?" — $49 a month, against the cost of two A+ vouchers to find out the hard way. The curriculum is genuinely broader than A+ prep: real Linux and sysadmin coverage that A+ barely touches, hands-on VM labs, and a Google brand that gets resume attention. Two concrete extras beyond the learning: it is ACE-approved for up to 15 college credits — the equivalent of five bachelor's-level courses, which matters if a degree is anywhere in your plan — and completers who go on to pass both A+ exams get a dual Google and CompTIA credential badge. Over 2.1 million people have enrolled; the honest way to be one of the minority who finish is to treat it like a scheduled class, not a someday hobby.
when_to_get_it: At the very start — before A+, not instead of it. The sequence most people settle on is the Google certificate first for the learning experience, then A+ for the resume line, listing both. Skip the Google certificate if you already have hands-on IT exposure: go straight to A+ and put the money into vouchers. Google has at times emailed completers a CompTIA exam discount, but neither Google nor Coursera advertises one today — budget for A+ at full price and treat any offer that arrives as a bonus rather than part of the plan.
salary_note: Google's '$70,000 median for IT support jobs' covers zero-to-five years of experience — don't expect it on offer one. Honest first-job numbers: BLS median for computer support specialists is $59,660 across all experience levels; ZipRecruiter averages ~$48K for help desk technicians; PayScale puts sub-1-year IT support at ~$46K. Realistic first role: $38–55K in most U.S. markets, $55–65K in high-cost metros — with real jumps in years 1–3 as you move toward desktop support and sysadmin work.
exam_duration: Self-paced — Coursera lists 6 courses at 3 months, 10 hours a week; Google says three-to-six months. Anyone with IT exposure finishes far faster
exam_format: No proctored exam. Six self-paced Coursera courses with auto-graded quizzes and hands-on Qwiklabs — browser-based VMs for real Linux, Windows, and networking exercises.
exam_questions: No final exam — graded quizzes and hands-on labs throughout
recertification_note: Never expires — course-completion certificate with a permanent Credly badge, no renewal cycle or fees. Employers accordingly read it as training evidence; the A+ pairing, and its dual badge, is what adds exam-tested weight.

study_steps.title: Audit course one free before subscribing
study_steps.description: Audit 'Technical Support Fundamentals' at no cost — all videos and readings, no graded labs. If it holds your attention for two weeks, subscribe. If money is the blocker, apply for Coursera financial aid (~15-day review) and get the whole program free.

study_steps.title: Set a 3-month pace before the trial starts
study_steps.description: The single biggest failure mode isn't difficulty — it's drift. Only ~14% of U.S. Coursera learners finish certificates they start. Block ten hours a week on your calendar; at that pace you're done in ~3 months (~$147 total) instead of paying $49/month indefinitely.

study_steps.title: Do every Qwiklab like it's a ticket
study_steps.description: The browser VMs are the program's real value — actual Linux and Windows practice, not videos about them. Treat each lab as a help-desk ticket: read it, solve it, and write one line about what you did. That habit is the job.

study_steps.title: Give courses 3 and 4 extra weight
study_steps.description: Operating Systems and System Administration are where this program genuinely outteaches A+ prep — the Linux and directory-services material is what separates 'help desk forever' from 'help desk, then sysadmin.' Slow down there.

study_steps.title: Claim the dual badge, then book A+
study_steps.description: Completion also unlocks up to 15 ACE-recommended college credits, worth claiming if a degree is on your horizon. Then book A+: passing both exams earns a dual Google and CompTIA Credly badge.

study_steps.title: Bridge to A+ with Professor Messer
study_steps.description: The Google cert taught concepts; A+ tests them under proctored pressure with its own exam vocabulary. Professor Messer's free Core 1/Core 2 series plus a $20 practice-exam bank closes that gap. Aim for consistent 85%+ on practice exams before booking either voucher.

study_steps.title: Apply while you study — don't wait for perfect
study_steps.description: Help desk hiring values availability, communication, and any customer-service history alongside credentials. Start applying once the Google cert is done and A+ study is underway — 'A+ in progress' with the Google cert on the resume is a legitimate, common entry position.

voucher_links.label: Enroll – Google IT Support on Coursera
voucher_links.note: No exam voucher exists — this is a Coursera subscription. Coursera charges $49 per month in the US and Canada after a 7-day free trial, and says most learners finish for under $300; the price is lower in some other countries. Financial aid can waive it entirely. The credential that costs money comes later: two CompTIA A+ exams, bought separately.

faq.question: Google IT Support Certificate or CompTIA A+ — which one first?
faq.answer: Both, in that order — that's the settled 2026 consensus. The Google cert is the better learning experience (broader, cheaper, hands-on VMs, actual Linux); A+ is the better resume line (it appears in ~65% of support listings, while almost none require the Google cert by name). Do the Google cert, then pass both A+ exams — that combination earns a dual Google and CompTIA badge, and it is the pairing support employers recognise.

faq.question: Can this certificate alone get me hired?
faq.answer: Sometimes, for the right person — help desk is the one genuinely entry-level IT tier, and hiring managers respect the cert as proof you can learn and finish. But a candidate with A+ plus any customer-service history usually beats a Google-cert-only resume. Treat it as the on-ramp that starts the engine, with A+ as the credential that clears the filters.

faq.question: How much does it really cost?
faq.answer: $49/month after the 7-day trial. Content is ~80–115 hours: finish in Google's 3-month estimate and it's ~$147; drift to the more realistic 6 months and it's ~$294. Financial aid can make it free. Budget for two A+ vouchers on top at CompTIA's current store price; Google does not currently advertise a discount on them, so plan without one.

faq.question: What's the employer consortium worth?
faq.answer: Access, not offers: 150+ U.S. employers (Deloitte, Target, Verizon, Wells Fargo, AT&T, Google itself) agree to consider graduates, via a job board for completers. It's a real perk and a bad reason to enroll — the coursework and the A+ bridge are the reasons.

faq.question: Is there college credit?
faq.answer: Yes — one of the largest ACE recommendations among Google certs: up to 15 U.S. college credits (about five bachelor-level courses) at participating schools, though acceptance is each school's call. If a degree is anywhere in your future plans, claim the Credly badge and keep it.

faq.question: Does it expire?
faq.answer: No — permanent course-completion certificate, no renewal or fees. Pair it with A+ (renewable, exam-tested) and you cover both what employers respect and what filters require.
